articles.title: Handling Legacy Domain Requests on a Static Site with 301 and 410
articles.excerpt: An inherited set of URLs Imperial Seedlings Guide is a static site built with Astro 5 and served from Cloudflare Pages. The domain previously belonged to a hemp seedling store from about 2020 to 2024…
articles.body: An inherited set of URLs Imperial Seedlings Guide is a static site built with Astro 5 and served from Cloudflare Pages. The domain previously belonged to a hemp seedling store from about 2020 to 2024 and has no connection to the current guide. The old site left a split set of URLs. 74 archived blog, product and archive pages now 301 to the closest guide. 263 cart, feed, plugin and script addresses answer 410 Gone. What the two status codes mean A 301 is a permanent redirect. It tells the browser or other HTTP client that the resource has moved and that future requests should go to the new location. The client may update stored bookmarks and will normally use the new address on the next visit. A 410 means the resource is gone.

articles.title: Logistics Renewal Webhooks: FIFO Queue Deduplication with Idempotency Keys After 5 Minutes
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a FIFO queue with an idempotency key to suppress rapid duplicate publishes, then make the webhook consumer idempotent in durable storage. The FIFO dedupe window is only 5 minutes, so…
articles.body: Short answer: use a FIFO queue with an idempotency key to suppress rapid duplicate publishes, then make the webhook consumer idempotent in durable storage. The FIFO dedupe window is only 5 minutes, so a renewal reminder that is retried later still needs an application-level record. I care about the boundary because delayed work tends to fail in the least convenient place. In logistics, a renewal reminder might wait until a carrier contract deadline, enter a queue, and eventually call a customer webhook. The queue can accept the work correctly while the delivery path retries it twice. The customer still sees two reminders. That is not a queue-selection problem alone.

articles.title: Eliminating Event Loop Contention in Python Async APIs Using Bounded Process Pools
articles.excerpt: Event Loop Starvation in CPU-Bound Python Workloads A frequent architectural misconception when designing asynchronous Python services with FastAPI or aiohttp is assuming that declaring async endpoint…
articles.body: Event Loop Starvation in CPU-Bound Python Workloads A frequent architectural misconception when designing asynchronous Python services with FastAPI or aiohttp is assuming that declaring async endpoints guarantees non-blocking execution across all workloads. While asyncio provides high-concurrency cooperative multitasking for I/O-bound operations (database sockets, external HTTP requests, and network streams), the event loop executes on a single OS thread . Whenever an async coroutine invokes synchronous CPU-bound operations—such as deserializing large payloads, executing local computer vision inference, or rendering binary reports—the event loop blocks entirely. All concurrent I/O callbacks and incoming requests are starved until the synchronous CPU execution completes.

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.
articles.body: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

articles.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
articles.excerpt: For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.
articles.body: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

articles.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
articles.excerpt: Rocket Lab has raised the launch cost of its next-gen Neutron rocket by more than 25%, an increase that reflects high demand amid a looming liftoff bottleneck.
articles.body: The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call.
